papers.title: Loss Mechanisms in High-coherence Multimode Mechanical Resonators Coupled to Superconducting Circuits
papers.abstract: Circuit quantum acoustodynamics (cQAD) devices have a wide range of applications in quantum science, all of which depend crucially on the quantum coherence of the mechanical subsystem. In this context, high-overtone bulk acoustic-wave resonators (HBARs) are particularly promising, since they have shown very high quality factors with negligible dephasing. However, the introduction of piezoelectric films, which are necessary for coupling to a superconducting circuit, can lead to additional loss channels, such as surface scattering and two-level systems (TLS). Here, we study the acoustic dissipation of HBAR resonators in cQAD systems and find that the defect density of the piezoelectric material and its interface with the bulk are limiting factors for the coherence. We measure acoustic modes with phonon lifetimes up to 400 $μ$s and lifetime-limited coherence times approaching one millisecond in the quantum regime. When coupled to a superconducting qubit, this leads to a hybrid system with a large quantum coherence cooperativity of $C_{T_2}=1.1\times10^5$. These results represent a new milestone for the performance of cQAD devices and offer concrete paths forward for further improvements.

summary.summary: This work studies dissipation mechanisms in high-overtone bulk acoustic-wave resonators (HBARs) coupled to superconducting qubits, finding that defect density in the piezoelectric AlN layer and its interface with sapphire limit coherence. The devices achieve phonon lifetimes of 396 µs and mechanical coherence times approaching 806 µs in the quantum regime, yielding a record cooperativity $C_{T_2} = 1.1 	imes 10^5$ for circuit quantum acoustodynamics.
summary.motivation: Quantum applications of mechanical resonators require both high coherence times and strong coupling to superconducting qubits, but adding piezoelectric films introduces loss channels that degrade performance. Understanding these loss mechanisms is essential for improving cQAD systems beyond current platforms.
summary.method: Multi-sample spectroscopy and qubit-based measurements characterized acoustic modes across 4–9 GHz in AlN-sapphire HBARs grown by three methods (sputtering, HVPE, HiPIMS). Energy participation analysis decomposed dissipation into mechanical absorption, surface scattering, and two-level system coupling; temperature and power sweeps isolated TLS effects from other loss channels.
summary.result: Single-phonon quality factors exceed $10^6$ in nearly all modes with record values $Q = 1.3 	imes 10^7$; lifetime-limited $T_2^* 	o 2T_1$ indicates negligible dephasing. HVPE-grown AlN shows five-fold lower TLS loss tangent ($Q_{TLS}^{-1} = 1.27 	imes 10^{-5}$) than sputtered AlN, but a $	ilde{10}$ nm interface defect layer with $Q_D^{-1} 	o 10^{-3}$ limits HVPE devices; smoother interfaces in sputtered samples achieve $f 	imes Q = 1.8 	imes 10^{17}$ Hz.

papers.title: Teleportation transition of surface codes on a superconducting quantum processor
papers.abstract: The topological surface code is a leading candidate for harnessing long-range entanglement to protect logical quantum information against errors, and teleportation of logical states is desirable for robust quantum information processing. Nevertheless, scaling up the surface code in quantum teleportation poses a formidable challenge to experiment. Here on a superconducting quantum processor with 125 qubits, we demonstrate the robust teleportation of topological rotated surface code prepared by a linear-depth unitary circuit, with code distances up to 7. We obtain the teleportation phase diagram by tuning the local entangling gates uniformly across a finite threshold. Furthermore, we show that the entangling threshold can be boosted by coherent qubit rotations that inject magic resources beyond the Clifford regime, restoring the duality symmetry of the topological phase, which serves as a guiding principle to minimize the entanglement resource. Our results shed light on simulating and leveraging topological quantum matter on quantum devices, and pave the way to the ultimate goal of distributed fault tolerant quantum computation.

similar_to.title: Logic gates at the surface code threshold: Superconducting qubits poised for fault-tolerant quantum computing

summary.summary: This work demonstrates teleportation of distance-7 topological surface codes on a 125-qubit superconducting processor, mapping out the phase diagram by tuning coherent errors and showing that the teleportation threshold increases from $0.122(2)\pi$ (at $\theta=\pi/2$) to $0.175(5)\pi$ (at $\theta=\pi/4$) through electric–magnetic duality symmetry. The experiment achieves logical error rates of $0.025(3)$ for Bob's teleported qubits and successfully teleports arbitrary logical states including magic states, validating operation below threshold with single-qubit gate fidelity 99.94% and two-qubit gate fidelity 99.64%.
summary.motivation: Scaling surface codes for fault-tolerant quantum computation requires demonstrating robust teleportation of topological logical qubits across imperfect entanglement resources, which has not been experimentally verified at meaningful code distances despite being essential for distributed quantum computing architectures.
summary.method: A tunable two-party state transfer protocol was implemented where Alice's distance-$d$ surface code (49 qubits per code) is teleported to Bob's initially product state by injecting coherent errors via parameterized $R_{XX}(\pi/2-2t)$ gates and single-qubit rotations $U(\theta,\phi)$, with tensor-network maximum-likelihood decoding applied to extract logical observables and measure phase transitions.
summary.result: Below threshold at $t=0$, Bob recovers logical states with mean parity $0.68(8)$ and logical error rate $0.025(3)$; the coherent error threshold reached $t_c^{\text{exp}}(\theta=\pi/2)=0.122(2)\pi$ versus ideal $0.107\pi$, and increased 43% to $t_c^{\text{exp}}(\theta=\pi/4)=0.175(5)\pi$ at the self-dual point, with averaged magic-state fidelity $0.95(2)$ post-teleportation.

papers.title: Beyond Single-Shot Fidelity: Chernoff-Based Throughput Optimization in Superconducting Qubit Readout
papers.abstract: Single-shot fidelity is the standard benchmark for superconducting qubit readout, yet it does not directly minimize the wall-clock time needed to certify a quantum state. We treat the dispersive measurement record as a stochastic communication channel and compute the classical Chernoff information governing the multi-shot error exponent, using a trajectory model that incorporates T1 relaxation with full cavity memory. The integration time that maximizes single-shot fidelity and the time that minimizes total certification time do not coincide. For representative transmon parameters and hardware overheads, the throughput-optimal window is longer, cutting certification time by roughly 9-11%, with the gain saturating near 1.13x in the high-readout-power and high-overhead regime. Benchmarking the extracted classical information against the unit-efficiency Gaussian Chernoff limit defines an information-extraction efficiency: dispersive schemes capture ~45% at short integration times, dropping to eta_info(tau_rate) ~ 12% at tau_rate ~ 1.22 us as T1-induced trajectory smearing accumulates. These results connect readout calibration directly to the operational objective of minimizing certification time in high-throughput superconducting processors.

similar_to.title: System Characterization of Dispersive Readout in Superconducting Qubits

summary.summary: This work reframes superconducting qubit readout optimization from maximizing single-shot fidelity to minimizing wall-clock certification time by treating dispersive measurement as a stochastic communication channel governed by classical Chernoff information. For transmon parameters with $\chi/2\pi = 1.2$ MHz, $\kappa/2\pi = 5.0$ MHz, $n̄ = 80$, $\eta = 0.45$, and $T_1 = 30$ µs, the throughput-optimal integration time $\tau_\mathrm{rate} \approx 1.22$ µs exceeds the fidelity-optimal time $\tau_\mathrm{fid} \approx 0.78$ µs, yielding 9–11% certification speedups that saturate at 1.13× in high-power, high-overhead regimes.
summary.motivation: Single-shot fidelity optimization does not minimize total certification time in high-throughput processors because it ignores the amortization of fixed per-shot hardware overheads ($\tau_\mathrm{oh} \sim 15$ µs) across multiple measurement shots.
summary.method: A trajectory model with full cavity memory incorporating stochastic $T_1$ relaxation computes classical Chernoff information $C(\tau)$ from matched-filter score distributions; total certification time $T_\mathrm{cert}(\tau) = [\log(1/\epsilon)/C(\tau)](\tau + \tau_\mathrm{oh})$ is then numerically minimized. An information-extraction efficiency metric $\eta_\mathrm{info}(\tau) = C(\tau)/C_\mathrm{ideal}(\tau)$ benchmarks performance against a unit-efficiency Gaussian limit.
summary.result: Information-extraction efficiency reaches ~45% at short integration times but drops to $\eta_\mathrm{info}(1.22 \text{ µs}) \approx 0.12$ at the throughput-optimal point due to $T_1$-induced trajectory smearing; this systematic separation between $\tau_\mathrm{fid}$ and $\tau_\mathrm{rate}$ persists even in the $T_1 \to \infty$ limit, proving it is a structural consequence of non-zero overhead rather than decoherence alone.

papers.title: Computing with many encoded logical qubits beyond break-even
papers.abstract: High-rate quantum error correcting (QEC) codes encode many logical qubits in a given number of physical qubits, making them promising candidates for quantum computation. Implementing high-rate codes at a scale that both frustrates classical computing and improves performance by encoding requires both high fidelity gates and long-range qubit connectivity -- both of which are offered by trapped-ion quantum computers. Here, we demonstrate computations that outperform their unencoded counterparts in the high-rate $[[ k+2,\, k,\, 2 ]]$ iceberg quantum error detecting (QED) and $[[ (k_2 + 2)(k_1 + 2),\, k_2k_1,\, 4 ]]$ two-level concatenated iceberg QEC codes, using the 98-qubit Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. Utilizing new gadgets for encoded operations, we realize this "beyond break-even" performance with reasonable postselection rates across a range of fault-tolerant (FT) and partially-fault-tolerant (pFT) component and application benchmarks with between $48$ and $94$ logical qubits. These benchmarks include FT state preparation and measurement, QEC cycle benchmarking, logical gate benchmarking, GHZ state preparation, and a pFT quantum simulation of the three-dimensional $XY$ model of quantum magnetism. Additionally, we illustrate that postselection rates can be suppressed by increasing the code distance via concatenation. Our results represent state-of-the-art logical component and state fidelities and provide evidence that high-rate QED/QEC codes are viable on contemporary quantum computers for near-term beyond-classical-scale computation.

similar_to.title: Breakeven demonstration of quantum low-density parity-check codes
Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit

summary.summary: This work demonstrates computations with many encoded logical qubits that outperform their unencoded counterparts using high-rate iceberg quantum error detecting and correcting codes on a trapped-ion quantum processor. Beyond-break-even performance is achieved with 48–94 logical qubits across benchmarks including state preparation, logical gates, GHZ state preparation, and partially fault-tolerant simulation of a three-dimensional $XY$ model.
summary.motivation: High-rate codes encode many logical qubits in fewer physical qubits, reducing overhead relative to surface codes, but their implementation at beyond-classical scale has remained challenging; trapped-ion platforms with arbitrary connectivity and high-fidelity gates enable realization of these codes.
summary.method: On the 98-qubit Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion processor with $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^+$ qubits and Mølmer–Sørensen $U_{ZZ}(\theta)$ gates, concatenated iceberg codes $[[k+2,k,2]]$ (distance-2) and $[[(k_2+2)(k_1+2),k_2k_1,4]]$ (distance-4) were implemented with new fault-tolerant and partially fault-tolerant gadgets for initialization, syndrome extraction, and logical gates, including GHZ-based syndrome extraction with four-qubit ancillary states and a log-depth state preparation circuit.
summary.result: SPAM infidelities per logical qubit improved by $\geq 10\times$ versus physical qubits ($3\times10^{-5}$ for distance-4 $[[80,48,4]]$); logical gate infidelities of $(1.0$–$1.2)\times10^{-4}$ outperformed bare two-qubit gate errors of $8\times10^{-4}$; GHZ state fidelities reached $\sim95\%$ in $\mathcal{I}_{94}$ codes; three-dimensional $XY$ model simulation on 64 logical qubits showed $\sim30\%$ reduction in effective two-qubit error rate ($\epsilon_{\sim 2Q} = 7.1(6)\times10^{-4}$ encoded versus $10.7(5)\times10^{-4}$ unencoded) with reasonable postselection rates.
